# Classically integrable defects {#sec-defect-conditions}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false title="Learning goals"}
- Write down the general first-order defect Lagrangian and its defect conditions, and see why energy is always conserved while momentum is a strong constraint.
- Derive the conditions for a conserved modified momentum, and show that under the type-I ansatz they single out $a_r^{(1)}$ with the defect matrix $\mathsf D=2(1-\pi)^{-1}$.
- Construct the defect matrix $L_d(\lambda)$ that intertwines the Lax pairs on the two sides, and use it to see that charges of both chiralities survive, which corrects the literature.
- Derive the Poisson bracket that the defect term of the action defines on independent defect values, and show that with it $L_d$ satisfies the Sklyanin bracket with the bulk r-matrix, so that the defect charges are in involution.
- Recognize the defect conditions as a frozen Bäcklund transformation, the defect matrix as its gauge transformation, and the delay of an $a_r$ soliton as its Bianchi coefficient.
- Know the type-II defects with an auxiliary field, the Tzitzéica defect, and the defects obtained by folding.
- Decide when a defect respects the antilinear symmetry $\Theta$.
:::

@sec-defect-sine-gordon treated the jump defect of sine-Gordon theory. This chapter asks which affine Toda theories admit such defects, and why the ones that do are integrable. The answer is more restrictive than for boundaries. Every affine Toda theory has integrable boundary conditions (@tbl-durham), but a defect that couples the two half-lines through first-order conditions, with no degrees of freedom of its own, exists only for $a_r^{(1)}$ [@bcz2004b; @cz2009a]. The criterion is momentum conservation: a defect breaks translation invariance, and asking for a modified momentum to survive leads to the same conditions as the existence of a Lax pair. Other algebras need a defect with an auxiliary field, the type-II defects of Corrigan and Zambon [-@cz2009b], and these are known only case by case.

The chapter mirrors @sec-boundary-conditions. A Lagrangian and its conditions come first, then the criterion that selects the integrable ones, the Lax matrix, and the r-matrix structure. Two calculations need particular attention. Both chiralities of conserved charges survive a type-I defect, contrary to a claim in the literature (@prp-spin-two). And the defect term of the action defines a finite-dimensional symplectic form on independent defect values; with its inverse bracket, the defect matrix satisfies the Sklyanin bracket with exactly the bulk r-matrix (@prp-defect-involution). How this finite-dimensional algebra relates to the equal-time Poisson structure of the whole field theory is discussed in @sec-defect-r-matrix. Everything is classical. The solutions are the subject of @sec-defect-solitons and the quantum theory that of @sec-defect-qg.

## The defect Lagrangian {#sec-defect-lagrangian}

The field is $\vec\phi$ on $x<0$ and $\vec\psi$ on $x>0$, each with the bulk Lagrangian $\mathcal L$ of @sec-lagrangians and its potential $V$ (-@eq-imaginary-potential). A defect at $x=0$ that is linear in time derivatives and contains no derivatives in $x$ has the action [@bcz2004b, eq. (3.1)]

$$
S=\int dt\,\Big\{\int_{-\infty}^0\mathcal L(\vec\phi)\,dx+\int_0^\infty\mathcal L(\vec\psi)\,dx+\Big[\tfrac12\vec\phi\cdot E\,\partial_t\vec\phi+\vec\phi\cdot\mathsf D\,\partial_t\vec\psi+\tfrac12\vec\psi\cdot F\,\partial_t\vec\psi-\mathcal B_d(\vec\phi,\vec\psi)\Big]_{x=0}\Big\},
$$ {#eq-defect-action}

with constant real matrices $E$, $F$ (antisymmetric, since symmetric parts are total derivatives) and $\mathsf D$, and a **defect potential** $\mathcal B_d$. The bulk boundary terms of the variation are $-\partial_x\vec\phi\cdot\delta\vec\phi$ from $x<0$ and $+\partial_x\vec\psi\cdot\delta\vec\psi$ from $x>0$, and the **defect conditions** are

$$
\partial_x\vec\phi=E\,\partial_t\vec\phi+\mathsf D\,\partial_t\vec\psi-\nabla_{\vec\phi}\mathcal B_d,\qquad
\partial_x\vec\psi=\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\partial_t\vec\phi-F\,\partial_t\vec\psi+\nabla_{\vec\psi}\mathcal B_d\qquad\text{at }x=0 .
$$ {#eq-defect-conditions}

The fields need not be continuous at $x=0$; this is a **jump defect**. Energy is always conserved. The bulk energy changes by $[\partial_t\vec\phi\cdot\partial_x\vec\phi-\partial_t\vec\psi\cdot\partial_x\vec\psi]_{x=0}$, and with (-@eq-defect-conditions) the terms quadratic in velocities cancel because $E$, $F$ are antisymmetric and the coefficient of $\partial_t\vec\psi$ in the first condition is the transpose of that of $\partial_t\vec\phi$ in the second. What remains is $-\frac d{dt}\mathcal B_d$, so $E+\mathcal B_d$ is conserved for every $\mathcal B_d$ (@exr-dc-energy). Corrigan and Zambon [-@cz2009a, eq. (2.6)] showed that these matrix properties are also necessary if the conditions are to conserve a modified energy.

**The type-I defects of $a_r^{(1)}$.** @sec-defect-momentum shows that a modified momentum is conserved only if, after a rotation of $\vec\psi$, $F=E=1-\mathsf D$ with $\mathsf D+\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}=2$, and that this requires $a_r^{(1)}$. Label the affine roots cyclically, $\vec\alpha_j=e_j-e_{j+1}$ in $\mathbb R^h$ ($j$ mod $h=r+1$), let $\vec\lambda_i$ ($i=1,\dots,r$) be the fundamental weights, with $\vec\lambda_0=\vec\lambda_{r+1}=0$, and let $\pi$ be the rotation of the diagram, $\pi\vec\alpha_j=\vec\alpha_{j-1}$. (The arrow distinguishes the weights from the spectral parameter $\lambda$.) Then

$$
\mathsf D=2\sum_{i=1}^r(\vec\lambda_i-\vec\lambda_{i+1})\vec\lambda_i^{\mathsf T}=2(1-\pi)^{-1},\qquad
E=F=1-\mathsf D=\sum_{i=1}^r\big(\vec\lambda_{i+1}\vec\lambda_i^{\mathsf T}-\vec\lambda_i\vec\lambda_{i+1}^{\mathsf T}\big),
$$ {#eq-d-matrix}

with $\vec\alpha_i\cdot\mathsf D\vec\alpha_j=2\delta_{ij}-2\delta_{i,j+1}$ and $\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\alpha_j=-\mathsf D\vec\alpha_{j-1}$ [@bcz2004b, eqs. (3.27)–(3.30)]. On the eigenvector of $\pi$ with eigenvalue $e^{2\pi ik/h}$, $k=1,\dots,r$, the matrix $\mathsf D$ is the number $2/(1-e^{2\pi ik/h})=1+i\cot\frac{\pi k}h$ (@exr-dc-d-matrix). For $a_1^{(1)}$, $\mathsf D=1$ and $E=0$, which is (-@eq-sg-defect-lagrangian). The **defect potential** is

$$
\mathcal B_d=\frac m{b^2}\sum_{j=0}^r\Big[\sigma\,(f_j-1)+\sigma^{-1}(g_j-1)\Big],\qquad
f_j=e^{b\vec\alpha_j\cdot(\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\phi+\mathsf D\vec\psi)/2},\quad g_j=e^{b\vec\alpha_j\cdot\mathsf D(\vec\phi-\vec\psi)/2},
$$ {#eq-defect-potential}

with $b=\beta$ at real and $b=i\beta$ at imaginary coupling, so that $\mathcal B_d^{\rm imag}$ follows from $\mathcal B_d^{\rm real}$ by $\beta\to i\beta$, as $V$ and the boundary potential do [@bcz2004b, eq. (3.32); @cz2007, eq. (2.10)]. The parameter is $\sigma=e^{-\theta_d}$, with $\theta_d$ the **defect rapidity** of @sec-sg-defect-lagrangian. This is the defect of **type I$_-$**, the one of Bowcock, Corrigan and Zambon. Its time reverse, **type I$_+$**, has $(\mathsf D,E)\to(-\mathsf D,-E)$ and $\sigma\leftrightarrow\sigma^{-1}$ in $\mathcal B_d$, with $\mathsf D$ in $f_j,g_j$ unchanged. The identities $f_jg_j=e^{b\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi}$ and $f_jg_{j+1}=e^{b\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\psi}$, consequences of $\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\alpha_{j+1}=-\mathsf D\vec\alpha_j$, are what make the defect integrable. All of this is checked in `code/defect_classical_an.py`.

**In components.** Realize the roots in $\mathbb R^h$, $h=r+1$, as $\vec\alpha_j=e_j-e_{j+1}$ with indices modulo $h$, so that $\pi e_k=e_{k-1}$, and let $\vec\mu_k=e_k-\frac1h\sum_le_l$ be the weights of the defining representation. The fields lie in the hyperplane of vectors whose components sum to zero, and their components are $\phi_k=\vec\mu_k\cdot\vec\phi$. Since $(1-\pi)\vec\mu_{j+1}=-\vec\alpha_j$, the defect matrix sends each root to a weight, $\mathsf D\vec\alpha_j=-2\vec\mu_{j+1}$ and $\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\alpha_j=2\vec\mu_j$, and

$$
f_j=e^{b(\psi_j-\phi_{j+1})},\qquad g_j=e^{b(\phi_j-\psi_j)} .
$$ {#eq-dc-components}

Each $f_j$ couples the field on the right at site $j$ with the field on the left at site $j+1$, and each $g_j$ is the jump at site $j$. The two identities above are then $f_jg_j=e^{b(\phi_j-\phi_{j+1})}$ and $f_jg_{j+1}=e^{b(\psi_j-\psi_{j+1})}$ (`code/defect_ar_partners.py`).

**The two types.** For $a_1^{(1)}$, type I$_+$ is type I$_-$ followed by $\psi\to-\psi$, a symmetry of the bulk (@sec-sg-defect-lagrangian). For $r\ge2$ the map $\psi\to-\psi$ is not a symmetry, because $-\vec\alpha_j$ is not an affine root, but reflections of the Dynkin diagram take its place. Let $\rho$ be the reflection $\rho\vec\alpha_j=\vec\alpha_{-j}$.

::: {#prp-dc-types}
## The two types are related by reflections
**[Theorem]** For both couplings and every $\sigma$,
$$
L_d^{\rm I_+}(\vec\phi,\vec\psi;\sigma)=L_d^{\rm I_-}\big(\rho\vec\phi,\rho\pi^{-1}\vec\psi;\sigma\big),
$$ {#eq-dc-types}
where $L_d=\frac12\vec\phi\cdot E\partial_t\vec\phi+\vec\phi\cdot\mathsf D\partial_t\vec\psi+\frac12\vec\psi\cdot F\partial_t\vec\psi-\mathcal B_d$ is the defect term of (-@eq-defect-action). So $(\vec\phi,\vec\psi)$ solves the type-I$_+$ conditions exactly when $(\rho\vec\phi,\rho\pi^{-1}\vec\psi)$ solves the type-I$_-$ conditions with the same $\sigma$: a type-I$_+$ defect is a type-I$_-$ defect seen through one reflection of the diagram on the left and another, $\rho\pi^{-1}$, on the right. In the same way $L_d^{\rm I_-}(\rho\vec\phi,\rho\vec\psi;\sigma)$ is the mirror image, with $\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}=2(1-\pi^{-1})^{-1}$ in place of $\mathsf D$.
:::

::: {.proof}
The reflection $\rho$ is orthogonal and permutes the affine roots, so it leaves $V$ invariant, and $\rho\pi\rho=\pi^{-1}$. Hence $\rho\mathsf D\rho=2(1-\pi^{-1})^{-1}=\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}$ and $\rho E\rho=1-\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}=-E$. The relation $\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\alpha_{j+1}=-\mathsf D\vec\alpha_j$ says $\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}=-\mathsf D\pi$. So the kinetic matrices of the right-hand side of (-@eq-dc-types) are $\rho E\rho=-E$, $\rho\mathsf D\rho\pi^{-1}=\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\pi^{-1}=-\mathsf D$ and $\pi\rho E\rho\pi^{-1}=-E$, those of type I$_+$. In components $(\rho\vec v)_k=-v_{1-k}$ and $(\pi^{-1}\vec v)_k=v_{k-1}$, so by (-@eq-dc-components) the map sends $f_j$ to $g_{-j}$ and $g_j$ to $f_{-j}$, which exchanges the coefficients $\sigma$ and $\sigma^{-1}$ of $\mathcal B_d$. For the mirror image, $\rho$ on both sides turns $\mathsf D$ into $\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}$ in the kinetic term and in $f_j$, $g_j$. The identity was checked for $h=2,\dots,5$ at both couplings, and type-I$_-$ soliton solutions mapped by $(\rho,\pi\rho)$ satisfy the type-I$_+$ conditions to $10^{-12}$ and violate the type-I$_-$ ones (`code/defect_ar_partners.py`).
:::

For $a_1^{(1)}$, $\rho=1$ and $\pi^{-1}=-1$, and (-@eq-dc-types) is the map $\psi\to-\psi$; its quantum form is part (3) of @prp-two-borels. For $r\ge2$ we have not worked out the quantum form. Penati and Polvara [-@penati_polvara2019, eqs. (3.16)–(3.17)] observed that the kinetic matrices of the two types are related by orthogonal transformations of the two fields. @prp-dc-types shows that these transformations can be chosen to be symmetries of the bulk, and then they also map one defect potential onto the other. The two types are related by time reversal as well. Together the two relations constrain which charges a defect keeps (@sec-defect-lax).

**Other first-order defects.** Bristow and Bowcock [-@bristow_bowcock2017, eq. (2.6)] wrote down the most general first-order defect Lagrangian with auxiliary fields $\vec\lambda(t)$ that live only at $x=0$: kinetic terms $\frac12\vec u\cdot A\vec u_t+\frac12\vec v\cdot B\vec v_t+\vec u\cdot C\vec v_t+\frac12\vec\lambda\cdot W\vec\lambda_t+\vec\lambda\cdot X\vec u_t+\vec\lambda\cdot Y\vec v_t$ and a potential $F(\vec u,\vec v,\vec\lambda)$. Field redefinitions reduce every such defect that conserves momentum to components coupled as in type I and components coupled through auxiliary fields as in the type-II defects of @sec-type-two-atft.

Entries are checked in `code/defect_classical_an.py` and `defect_classical_sg.py` unless marked "by hand". {#tbl-defect-dictionary}

## Momentum conservation as a criterion {#sec-defect-momentum}

The defect breaks translation invariance, so momentum is conserved only if the defect can absorb it. Corrigan and Zambon [-@cz2009a] turned this into a criterion that is easier to use than the spin-3 charge of @prp-sg-defect-classification. With $P=-\int_{-\infty}^0\partial_t\vec\phi\cdot\partial_x\vec\phi\,dx-\int_0^\infty\partial_t\vec\psi\cdot\partial_x\vec\psi\,dx$ and the bulk field equations,

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=\Big[\tfrac12(\partial_t\vec\psi)^2+\tfrac12(\partial_x\vec\psi)^2-V(\vec\psi)-\tfrac12(\partial_t\vec\phi)^2-\tfrac12(\partial_x\vec\phi)^2+V(\vec\phi)\Big]_{x=0}.
$$ {#eq-dc-momentum-flux}

Substitute (-@eq-defect-conditions). The result is a polynomial of degree two in the velocities, and $P+P_d$ is conserved for a function $P_d(\vec\phi,\vec\psi)$ exactly when the three parts match separately.

::: {#prp-defect-momentum}
## Conditions for momentum conservation
**[Established; numerically checked]** For the defect conditions (-@eq-defect-conditions), $P+P_d$ is conserved if and only if

1. (quadratic terms) $\mathsf D\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}=1-E^2$, $\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\mathsf D=1-F^2$ and $E\mathsf D=\mathsf DF$;
2. (linear terms) $\nabla_{\vec\phi}P_d=E\nabla_{\vec\phi}\mathcal B_d-\mathsf D\nabla_{\vec\psi}\mathcal B_d$ and $\nabla_{\vec\psi}P_d=-\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\nabla_{\vec\phi}\mathcal B_d-F\nabla_{\vec\psi}\mathcal B_d$;
3. (no velocities) $\frac12\lvert\nabla_{\vec\phi}\mathcal B_d\rvert^2-\frac12\lvert\nabla_{\vec\psi}\mathcal B_d\rvert^2=V(\vec\phi)-V(\vec\psi)$.

Condition 1 holds exactly when $\mathsf D=(1-E)O$ and $F=O^{\mathsf T}EO$ with $O$ orthogonal; after the rotation $\vec\psi\to O\vec\psi$ it becomes $\mathsf D=1-E$, $F=E$. For the $a_r^{(1)}$ defect (-@eq-d-matrix), (-@eq-defect-potential) of either type all three hold, with
$$
P_d^{\rm I_-}=-\frac m{b^2}\sum_{j=0}^r\Big[\sigma(f_j-1)-\sigma^{-1}(g_j-1)\Big],\qquad P_d^{\rm I_+}(\sigma)=-P_d^{\rm I_-}(1/\sigma).
$$
In light-cone form, $E+P$ (spin $+1$) acquires only the $\sigma^{-1}g_j$ terms and $E-P$ only the $\sigma f_j$ terms.
:::

::: {.proof}
The three parts of $\frac d{dt}(P+P_d)$ are those listed [@cz2009a, eqs. (2.7)–(2.9)], rewritten for the book's sign of $P$ and with $F$ in place of their $-D$. Since $E$ is real antisymmetric, $1-E$ is invertible and $\mathsf D\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}=(1-E)(1-E)^{\mathsf T}$ gives $O=(1-E)^{-1}\mathsf D$ orthogonal; then $E\mathsf D=\mathsf DF$ forces $F=O^{\mathsf T}EO$, and the second equation follows. For (-@eq-defect-potential), condition 3 follows from $f_jg_j=e^{b\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\phi}$ and $f_jg_{j+1}=e^{b\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec\psi}$: the cross terms of the squares give $\frac{m^2}{b^2}\sum_jf_j(g_j-g_{j+1})$, and the squares of the $f$ and $g$ terms cancel separately because $\mathsf D$ is normal. Condition 2 holds with the stated $P_d$ term by term: $E\mathsf D-\mathsf D\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}=-\mathsf D$ for the $f_j$ and $E+\mathsf D=1$ for the $g_j$. All three conditions, the gradient form of condition 2, and the conservation laws along the defect conditions are checked at random complex points for $r=1,\dots,4$, both couplings and both types (`code/defect_classical_an.py`).
:::

**The two halves.** Condition 2 can be solved without any ansatz. With $\mathsf D=1-E$ and $F=E$, use the coordinates

$$
\begin{aligned}
\vec\xi&=\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\phi+\mathsf D\vec\psi,&\vec\eta&=\vec\phi-\vec\psi;\\
\vec\phi&=\tfrac12\big(\vec\xi+\mathsf D\vec\eta\big),&\vec\psi&=\tfrac12\big(\vec\xi-\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\eta\big),
\end{aligned}
$$

where the inverse uses $\mathsf D+\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}=2$. Then $\nabla_{\vec\phi}=\mathsf D\nabla_{\vec\xi}+\nabla_{\vec\eta}$ and $\nabla_{\vec\psi}=\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\nabla_{\vec\xi}-\nabla_{\vec\eta}$, and, by $E\mathsf D-\mathsf D\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}=-\mathsf D$, $E+\mathsf D=1$, $\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\mathsf D+E\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}=\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}$ and $E-\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}=-1$, condition 2 becomes $\nabla_{\vec\xi}P_d=-\nabla_{\vec\xi}\mathcal B_d$ and $\nabla_{\vec\eta}P_d=\nabla_{\vec\eta}\mathcal B_d$. A function $P_d$ with these gradients exists exactly when $\partial^2\mathcal B_d/\partial\xi_a\partial\eta_b=0$ for all $a$, $b$. So

$$
\mathcal B_d=f(\vec\xi)+g(\vec\eta),\qquad P_d=g(\vec\eta)-f(\vec\xi),
$$ {#eq-dc-halves}

for two functions $f$ and $g$ of $r$ variables, as for sine-Gordon theory, where they are functions of $\phi+\psi$ and $\phi-\psi$ (-@eq-sg-defect-potential). The defect conditions then take the light-cone form

$$
\partial_+\big(\vec\phi-\vec\psi\big)=-2\nabla f(\vec\xi),\qquad\partial_-\big(\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\phi+\mathsf D\vec\psi\big)=2\nabla g(\vec\eta)\qquad\text{at }x=0,
$$ {#eq-dc-lightcone}

with $\partial_\pm=\partial_t\pm\partial_x$. Since $\mathsf D$ is normal, $|\nabla_{\vec\phi}\mathcal B_d|^2-|\nabla_{\vec\psi}\mathcal B_d|^2=4\nabla f\cdot\nabla g$, and condition 3 becomes $2\nabla f(\vec\xi)\cdot\nabla g(\vec\eta)=V(\vec\phi)-V(\vec\psi)$ (`code/defect_ar_partners.py`). For the $a_r^{(1)}$ defect (-@eq-defect-potential), $f$ is the half with $\sigma$ and $g$ the half with $\sigma^{-1}$, and the light-cone statement of @prp-defect-momentum is $\mathcal B_d+P_d=2g$ and $\mathcal B_d-P_d=2f$.

**The exponential ansatz.** The bulk potentials are sums of exponentials, so Corrigan and Zambon [-@cz2009a, eqs. (2.16)–(2.21)] took $\mathcal B_d$ to be a finite sum of exponentials $e^{\vec a\cdot\vec\phi+\vec b\cdot\vec\psi}$, with $\mathsf D=1-E$ and $F=E$. By (-@eq-dc-halves) each exponential depends on $\vec\xi$ or on $\vec\eta$ alone, so there are only two kinds: $f_{\vec x}=e^{b\vec x\cdot(\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\phi+\mathsf D\vec\psi)/2}$ in $f$ and $g_{\vec y}=e^{b\vec y\cdot(\vec\phi-\vec\psi)/2}$ in $g$. In $2\nabla f\cdot\nabla g$ a product $f_{\vec x}g_{\vec y}$ appears with the coefficient $\frac{b^2}2\vec x\cdot\vec y$ times the product of the two coefficients. It is a bulk exponential $e^{b\vec\alpha\cdot\vec\phi}$ only if $\vec x=\vec\alpha$, $\vec y=\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\alpha$, and $e^{b\vec\alpha\cdot\vec\psi}$ only if $\vec x=\vec\alpha$, $\vec y=-\mathsf D\vec\alpha$. Assume, as Corrigan and Zambon do, that the same affine Toda theory sits on both sides with the same roots after the rotation that set $\mathsf D=1-E$. Then the $f$ exponents are the roots $\vec\alpha_j$, and every unwanted product must have $\vec x\cdot\vec y=0$.

One more step makes this a statement about automorphisms. If some $\vec y=\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\alpha_i$ had no partner among the $-\mathsf D\vec\alpha_k$, it would have to be orthogonal to every $\vec\alpha_j$ with $j\ne i$, hence, since $\sum_jn_j\vec\alpha_j=0$, to $\vec\alpha_i$ as well, contradicting $\vec\alpha_i\cdot\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\alpha_i=\vec\alpha_i^2$. So there is a fixed-point-free permutation $p$ of the nodes with $\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\alpha_i=-\mathsf D\vec\alpha_{p(i)}$, that is $\mathsf D(\vec\alpha_i-\vec\alpha_{p(i)})=2\vec\alpha_i$. The linear map $P:\vec\alpha_i\mapsto\vec\alpha_{p(i)}$ exists because $\mathsf D$ is invertible, it is orthogonal because $\mathsf D+\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}=2$, so $p$ is an automorphism of the affine Dynkin diagram, and

$$
\mathsf D=2(1-P)^{-1},\qquad\vec\alpha_i\cdot\mathsf D\vec\alpha_j=0\quad\text{for }j\notin\{i,p(i)\}
$$

[@bcz2004b, eqs. (3.19)–(3.24)]. Each $p$-orbit of nodes carries one free parameter: the terms $e^{b\vec\alpha_i\cdot\vec\phi}$ and $e^{b\vec\alpha_i\cdot\vec\psi}$ of $V$ come from the products of $f_{\vec\alpha_i}$ with $g_{\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\alpha_i}$ and with $g_{-\mathsf D\vec\alpha_i}=g_{\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\alpha_{p^{-1}(i)}}$, their coefficients must be opposite, and so the coefficients of $g$ are constant on the orbits of $p$. The second condition is the strong one, and it can be tested diagram by diagram.

::: {#prp-ar-only}
## Only $a_r^{(1)}$ has type-I defects
**[Theorem]** Under the assumptions just stated (constant real matrices, the same theory and the same roots on both sides after the rotation, and $\mathcal B_d$ a finite sum of exponentials), a modified momentum is conserved only for $a_r^{(1)}$, with $P=\pi$ or $\pi^{-1}$. Then $\mathcal B_d$ is (-@eq-defect-potential), or its mirror image with $\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}=2(1-\pi^{-1})^{-1}$, which is the same defect after relabelling $j\to-j$. For every affine Dynkin diagram of rank at most 4, untwisted and twisted, and every one of its automorphisms, the scan confirms this: only $\pi^{\pm1}$ of $a_r^{(1)}$ pass.
:::

::: {.proof}
The text above reduces the question to a symmetry $p$ of the diagram without fixed nodes and the condition $\vec\alpha_i\cdot\mathsf D\vec\alpha_j=0$ for $j\notin\{i,p(i)\}$. One more step settles it. Let $k$ be a neighbour of the node $i$, so that $k\ne i$ and $\vec\alpha_k\cdot\vec\alpha_i\ne0$. The scalar product of $\mathsf D(\vec\alpha_i-\vec\alpha_{p(i)})=2\vec\alpha_i$ with $\vec\alpha_k$ is $\vec\alpha_k\cdot\mathsf D\vec\alpha_i-\vec\alpha_k\cdot\mathsf D\vec\alpha_{p(i)}=2\vec\alpha_k\cdot\vec\alpha_i\ne0$. By the condition, the first term can be nonzero only if $i=p(k)$, and the second only if $p(i)=k$, since $p(i)=p(k)$ would give $k=i$. So every neighbour of $i$ is $p(i)$ or $p^{-1}(i)$. Each node therefore has at most two neighbours, and they lie on its $p$-orbit. The diagram is connected, so $p$ has a single orbit. Each node $i$ has a neighbour, so it is joined to $p(i)$: if it is joined to $p^{-1}(i)$, apply $p$. The diagram is therefore the closed path $i\to p(i)\to p^2(i)\to\cdots$ through all $h=r+1$ nodes, with no other edges. For $h\ge3$ the only affine Dynkin diagram that contains a cycle is that of $a_r^{(1)}$, and $p$ moves each node one step along it, so $p=\pi^{\pm1}$. For $h=2$ the two nodes are exchanged, so they have equal length, and the diagram is $a_1^{(1)}$. With a single orbit all coefficients of $g$ are equal, those of $f$ follow from the coefficients of $V$, and $\mathcal B_d$ is (-@eq-defect-potential) with one parameter $\sigma$, up to a constant, or its mirror image for $p=\pi^{-1}$. This is the argument of Corrigan and Zambon [-@cz2009a, eqs. (2.30)–(2.35)], who count the neighbours of a node with fundamental weights, written in terms of the symmetry $p$.

The other diagrams fail in recognizable ways. If $p$ has more than one orbit, then for each orbit $O$ the vector $\sum_{j\in O}\vec\alpha_j$ is fixed by $P$, and it is nonzero because the only linear relation among the affine roots, $\sum_jn_j\vec\alpha_j=0$, involves all of them with positive coefficients; so $1-P$ is singular. A tree has a centre, a node or an edge fixed by every automorphism, so on a tree with three or more nodes a symmetry without fixed nodes exchanges the ends of a central edge and has more than one orbit. And the rotations $\pi^k$ of $a_r^{(1)}$ with $k\ne\pm1$ coprime to $h$ fail the neighbour property. The scan in `code/defect_classical_an.py` confirms this without the argument. It runs through 23 diagrams ($a_1^{(1)},\dots,a_4^{(1)}$, $b_3^{(1)}$, $b_4^{(1)}$, $c_2^{(1)},\dots,c_4^{(1)}$, $d_4^{(1)}$, $f_4^{(1)}$, $g_2^{(1)}$, $a_2^{(2)}$, $a_4^{(2)}$, $a_6^{(2)}$, $a_8^{(2)}$, $a_3^{(2)}=d_3^{(2)}$, $a_5^{(2)}$, $a_7^{(2)}$, $d_4^{(2)}$, $d_5^{(2)}$, $e_6^{(2)}$, $d_4^{(3)}$) and their 78 automorphisms. In 64 cases $p$ fixes a node. In 5 cases $1-P$ is singular: the two reflections of $a_3^{(1)}$ that fix no node, the rotation $\pi^2$ of $a_3^{(1)}$, and the reversals of $c_3^{(1)}$ and $d_4^{(2)}$. The rotations $\pi^{\pm2}$ of $a_4^{(1)}$ produce ten forbidden cross terms each, and leave a residual of order 1 in condition 3. The remaining 7 automorphisms, $\pi^{\pm1}$ of $a_r^{(1)}$, $r=2,3,4$, and the exchange of the two nodes of $a_1^{(1)}$, pass, and condition 3 then holds at random points to $10^{-15}$. An independent scan in `code/defect_ar_partners.py` finds the same numbers and checks, case by case, that the condition holds exactly when every neighbour of each node is its partner or the node whose partner it is.
:::

Two features of the answer stand out. Every other affine Toda theory, including the folded ones whose solitons are images of $a_r^{(1)}$ solitons, has no type-I defect. And the obstruction is combinatorial: the defect matrix must come from an automorphism that cycles through all the nodes, and a potential without unwanted cross terms then needs every neighbour of a node to be its partner or the node whose partner it is, so that the cycle is the diagram itself. Corrigan and Zambon [-@cz2009a, eqs. (2.42)–(2.44)] also found that a defect may join different theories, because conformal Toda theory has no affine root: an $a_r$ conformal Toda theory on the left and an $a_{r-1}$ conformal Toda theory plus a free massless field on the right, so that $r$ defects in a row reduce conformal Toda theory to free fields.

Is momentum conservation enough for integrability? For type I it is. @sec-defect-lax constructs a Lax pair for exactly these defects, and a non-integrable $\mathsf D$ admits none. For the type-II defects of @sec-type-two-atft, Bristow [-@bristow2017, Sec. 3] constructed defect Lax matrices for the Tzitzéica defect and for a $d_4^{(1)}$ defect, and in both cases momentum conservation was exactly what was needed.

::: {#cnj-momentum-integrability}
## Momentum conservation and integrability
**[Conjecture]** A first-order defect in affine Toda theory, with or without auxiliary fields, is classically integrable, in the sense that it admits a defect Lax matrix and infinitely many conserved charges, if and only if it conserves a modified momentum.
:::

Bristow [-@bristow2017, Sec. 3.4] calls momentum conservation "very likely" necessary for integrability. The evidence is the type-I classification, the $a_1$, Tzitzéica and $d_4$ Lax matrices, and the fact that every momentum-conserving defect found so far is a Bäcklund transformation when imposed for all $x$ [@bristow_bowcock2017, Sec. 3]. The analogy with boundaries is instructive. At a boundary the energy is always conserved, so energy conservation selects nothing, and integrability is the much stronger condition of @sec-durham-classification; at a defect the energy is also free, but momentum is a genuine constraint, and the conjecture says it is the only one. In the quantum theory the analogy may fail: Penati and Polvara [-@penati_polvara2019, Sec. 5] found that a finite renormalization restores quantum momentum conservation but not the spin-3 charge (@cnj-defect-parameter).

## Lax pairs with a defect {#sec-defect-lax}

Bowcock, Corrigan and Zambon [-@bcz2004, Sec. 4; -@bcz2004b, Sec. 3] constructed the Lax pair of the defect theory from two Lax pairs on overlapping regions, $x<b$ for $\vec\phi$ and $x>a$ for $\vec\psi$, related by a gauge transformation in the overlap. Shrinking the overlap to the point $x=0$ leaves a single matrix. With $a_t=\frac12(\mathcal A_++\mathcal A_-)$ of (-@eq-boundary-lax-at), a solution $\Psi$ of $(\partial_t+a_t)\Psi=0$ on each side, and $\Psi_\phi=L_d\Psi_\psi$ at $x=0$, the **defect matrix** $L_d(\lambda)$ must satisfy

$$
\partial_tL_d=L_d\,a_t(\vec\psi)-a_t(\vec\phi)\,L_d\quad\text{at }x=0,\qquad
L_d(\lambda)=e^{-bH\cdot(E\vec\phi+\mathsf D\vec\psi)/2}\,\tilde L(\lambda)\,e^{bH\cdot(\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\phi-E\vec\psi)/2},
$$ {#eq-defect-lax-matrix}

with the defect conditions used to eliminate $\partial_x\vec\phi$, $\partial_x\vec\psi$, and $\tilde L(\lambda)$ independent of the fields. In the defining representation of $a_r^{(1)}$, where $E_{\vec\alpha_j}=e_{j,j+1}$ (indices mod $h$) and $S=\sum_jE_{\vec\alpha_j}$ is the cyclic permutation matrix,

$$
\tilde L_{\rm I_-}(\lambda)=1+\frac\sigma\lambda\sum_{j=0}^rE_{-\vec\alpha_j}=1+\frac\sigma\lambda S^{\mathsf T},\qquad
\tilde L_{\rm I_+}(\lambda)=\sum_{k=0}^{r}\Big(\frac\lambda\sigma\Big)^kS^k\ \propto\ \Big(1-\frac\lambda\sigma S\Big)^{-1}.
$$

For type I$_-$ the defect matrix simplifies to $L_d=e^{bH\cdot(\vec\phi-\vec\psi)/2}\big[1+\frac\sigma\lambda\sum_je^{b\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec w/2}E_{-\vec\alpha_j}\big]$ with $\vec w=\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}\vec\phi-E\vec\psi$: the Cartan factor sees only the jump $\vec\phi-\vec\psi$.

::: {#prp-defect-lax}
## The defect Lax matrix
**[Established; numerically checked for $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$]** For the $a_r^{(1)}$ defects (-@eq-d-matrix), (-@eq-defect-potential), the matrix (-@eq-defect-lax-matrix) satisfies its evolution equation on the defect conditions, for both couplings. In the defining representation the field-independent $\tilde L$ is unique up to a scalar factor, with the coefficient of $\sigma/\lambda$ exactly 1 in the normalization of @sec-lax-pair; this is eq. (3.39) of @bcz2004b with their $d=\sigma$ and their $\lambda$ equal to the book's. Within this field-independent ansatz the allowed matrices are (-@eq-d-matrix) and its transpose, the mirror image of @prp-ar-only, which is the same defect after the relabelling $j\to-j$; for any other $\mathsf D$ with $\mathsf D+\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}=2$ there is no field-independent $\tilde L$. On the vacuum, a soliton of rapidity $\theta$ corresponds to $\lambda=-e^{-\theta}$, so the off-diagonal part $\sigma/\lambda$ of $\tilde L_{\rm I_-}$ grows like $e^{\theta-\theta_d}$, as the conversion amplitude of @sec-sg-defect-solitons does.
:::

::: {.proof}
Substituting (-@eq-defect-lax-matrix) and the defect conditions, the evolution equation becomes a Laurent polynomial in $\lambda$ whose coefficients are sums of exponentials of the fields. Order by order in $1/\lambda$ it determines $\tilde L$ and forces (-@eq-d-matrix) and (-@eq-defect-potential) [@bcz2004b, eqs. (3.9)–(3.39)]. We solved the linear equations for $\tilde L$ numerically, stacked over random field configurations, for $r=1,2,3$, both couplings and both types, and found a one-dimensional solution space with the stated $\tilde L$, a one-dimensional space for the mirror image $(\mathsf D^{\mathsf T},-E)$, and none for $E\to0.6E$ (`code/defect_classical_an.py`).
:::

**Which charges survive.** Bowcock, Corrigan and Zambon [-@bcz2004b, Sec. 5] expected the "lack of balance between $\lambda$ and $1/\lambda$" in $\tilde L$ to distinguish the two chiralities, and concluded from the spin-$\pm2$ charges of $a_r^{(1)}$ that only one of them survives each type of defect; Penati and Polvara [-@penati_polvara2019, App. B] repeated the classical argument. Their argument was that the terms cubic in velocities in the defect flux of the lost charge are proportional to $A_{abc}(\mathsf D_{ap}\mathsf D_{bq}\mathsf D_{cr}+\mathsf D_{pa}\mathsf D_{qb}\mathsf D_{rc})$ [@bcz2004b, eq. (5.11)], with $A_{abc}$ the symmetric tensor of the cubic term of the bulk spin-2 density, and that this does not vanish "because of (3.20)", the relation $\mathsf D=2-\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}$. That inference is wrong, and so is the conclusion.

::: {#prp-spin-two}
## Both spin-two charges survive
**[Theorem for (1), and for $a_2^{(1)}$ and $a_3^{(1)}$ in (3); Proposition, sketch for (2) and all $a_r^{(1)}$]** For both types of defect, both the spin $+2$ and the spin $-2$ charges of $a_r^{(1)}$, $r\ge2$, survive, with local defect contributions. More generally, for every spin $s$ present in the bulk hierarchy, the charges of spin $+s$ and of spin $-s$ both survive separately, each with a local defect contribution.

1. The obstruction of @bcz2004b [eq. (5.11)] vanishes identically for every $r$.
2. The generating function $\tau_d(\lambda)$ of (-@eq-defect-monodromy) is conserved, and $L_d(\lambda)$, $L_d(\lambda)^{-1}$ have Laurent expansions with invertible leading coefficients both at $\lambda\to\infty$ and at $\lambda\to0$. Its expansions at the two ends give local charges of the two chiralities, each with a local defect contribution.
3. For $a_2^{(1)}$ and $a_3^{(1)}$ the defect flux of each spin-$\pm2$ charge is exactly the total time derivative of a local function $\mathcal B_{\pm2}$, for both types and every $\sigma$; $\mathcal B_{\pm2}$ are given explicitly for $a_2^{(1)}$ in `code/defect_classical_an.py` and for $a_3^{(1)}$ in `code/defect_spin_two_a3.py`.
:::

::: {.proof}
(1) In the normalization $T_{\pm3}=\frac13A_{abc}\partial_\pm\phi_a\partial_\pm\phi_b\partial_\pm\phi_c+B_{ab}\partial_\pm^2\phi_a\partial_\pm\phi_b$ of @bcz2004b [eq. (5.2)], the tensor is $A(\vec u,\vec u,\vec u)=2\sum_{k=1}^h(\vec\mu_k\cdot\vec u)^3$, with $\vec\mu_k$ the weights of the defining representation, so that the cubic term of the density is $\frac23\sum_k(\vec\mu_k\cdot\vec u)^3$; with $B=1-\mathsf D$ [@bcz2004b, eq. (5.6)] it solves their (5.5). Expand $\vec v$ in eigenvectors of $\pi$. The cubic invariant couples only modes with $k_1+k_2+k_3\equiv0$ mod $h$, and on them $\mathsf D=1+ic_i$ with $c_i=\cot\frac{\pi k_i}h$. The obstruction is a sum of terms $d_1d_2d_3+\bar d_1\bar d_2\bar d_3=2\big[1-(c_1c_2+c_2c_3+c_3c_1)\big]$, and $\cot a\cot b+\cot b\cot c+\cot c\cot a=1$ whenever $a+b+c\equiv0$ mod $\pi$ (@exr-dc-cot). So the obstruction vanishes, although each of its two terms does not. Polarization gives the same for the mixed cubic terms of @penati_polvara2019 [eq. (B.4)].

(2) The argument of @sec-conserved-charges applies on each half-line. At $\lambda\to\infty$ the Drinfeld–Sokolov gauge transformation $G(x;\lambda)$, a local series in $1/\lambda$, brings the transport matrices to $e^{-\int\mathfrak h\,dx}$ with $\mathfrak h$ in the principal Heisenberg subalgebra, whose coefficients are the bulk densities of one chirality [@drinfeld_sokolov1985; @olive1985]. Then $\tau_d=\operatorname{tr}\big(G^\psi(x_+)\,e^{-\int_0^{x_+}\mathfrak h^\psi}N(\lambda)\,e^{-\int_{x_-}^0\mathfrak h^\phi}G^\phi(x_-)^{-1}\big)$ with $N(\lambda)=G^\psi(0)^{-1}L_d(\lambda)^{-1}G^\phi(0)$, and for large $|\lambda|$ on a suitable ray one eigenvalue $k_*$ of $\mathfrak h$ dominates: $\ln\tau_d$ is the sum of the two bulk integrals and $\ln N_{k_*k_*}(\lambda)$. Since $L_d(\lambda)^{-1}$ tends to an invertible Cartan element, which is $1$ at the vacuum, the leading coefficient of $N$ is the identity at the vacuum; its diagonal entries are analytic in the defect values, so $N_{k_*k_*}$ has a nonzero leading term for generic defect values. (Invertibility alone would not suffice, since an invertible matrix can have zero diagonal entries.) Then $\ln N_{k_*k_*}$ is a series in $1/\lambda$ whose coefficients are functions of $\vec\phi(0)$, $\vec\psi(0)$ and finitely many derivatives; the $x$-derivatives reduce to $t$-derivatives through the defect conditions and the field equations. At $\lambda\to0$ the same argument uses the opposite gauge, in which $\lambda^{-1}S^{\mathsf T}$ dominates. Now $\tilde L_{\rm I_-}=\frac\sigma\lambda S^{\mathsf T}(1+\frac\lambda\sigma S)$, and $S^{\mathsf T}$ is invertible, so after the scalar factor $\sigma/\lambda$ the leading coefficient of $L_d^{-1}$ is $S$ dressed by Cartan elements. At the vacuum it is $S$ itself, diagonal in its eigenbasis with the $h$-th roots of unity on the diagonal, so by analyticity its diagonal entries in that basis are again nonzero for generic defect values. For type I$_+$, $\tilde L_{\rm I_+}^{-1}\propto1-\frac\lambda\sigma S$ is regular at both ends in the same way. Nothing couples the two ends of the $\lambda$-plane, unlike the double-row matrix (-@eq-double-row) of a boundary, which contains both $T(\lambda)$ and $T(1/\lambda)$ and therefore only the combinations $Q_s+Q_{-s}$. The invertibility statements are checked in `code/defect_lax_rmatrix.py`. What is not proved here: control of the dominant eigenvalue and of the regularized generating function on the infinite line, which is standard but not written out, and the reorganization of the expansion at exceptional defect values where the leading entry vanishes, which happens at imaginary coupling on special values of the jump. Hence the label "sketch".

(3) With the defect conditions, the flux of each charge through $x=0$ is a function of $\vec\phi(0,t)$, $\vec\psi(0,t)$ and their first three time derivatives. It is a total time derivative of a local function if and only if its Euler operator in $t$ vanishes. We evaluated the symbolic Euler operator at random points (residual $10^{-15}$), together with closed-loop integrals along random periodic paths. Controls: the spin-$\pm1$ fluxes pass, a non-integrable $\mathsf D$ fails, the bulk current is conserved on shell, and its density is not a total $x$-derivative. The homotopy formula then constructs $\mathcal B_{\pm2}$: both are linear in $\partial_t\vec\phi$, $\partial_t\vec\psi$ plus a sum of exponentials, and the flux minus $\frac d{dt}\mathcal B_{\pm2}$ simplifies to zero exactly, with $\sigma$ symbolic, for both types. This exact identity is what makes (3) a theorem for $a_2^{(1)}$. For type I$_-$, $\mathcal B_{+2}$ contains the velocities only multiplied by $\sigma^{-1}g_j$ and $\mathcal B_{-2}$ only multiplied by $\sigma f_j$, as for $E\pm P$ in @prp-defect-momentum (`code/defect_classical_an.py`). The same closed-form construction of $A_{abc}$ and the same homotopy formula, generalized from the hard-coded $a_2$ root system to a general-$r$ exact Gram–Schmidt basis, give the identical exact cancellation for $a_3^{(1)}$, with the same velocity structure, both types, $\sigma$ symbolic, with controls (the spin-$\pm1$ case passes; a non-integrable $\mathsf D$ fails) (`code/defect_spin_two_a3.py`, about three minutes, dominated by the non-integrable-$\mathsf D$ control).
:::

The two relations between the types also show why the conclusion of @bcz2004b [Sec. 5] could not hold for every $\sigma$. Time reversal maps the type-I$_-$ defect with $\sigma$ to the type-I$_+$ defect with $1/\sigma$, and a conserved charge of spin $s$ to one of spin $-s$. @prp-dc-types maps the type-I$_+$ defect back to the type-I$_-$ defect with the same $\sigma$, through the bulk symmetries $\rho$ and $\pi$, which keep the spin. Each exponent of $a_r^{(1)}$ has multiplicity one, so $\rho$ multiplies each local bulk charge of a given spin by a nonzero number. The rotation $\pi$ leaves every charge in the local hierarchy invariant: with the cyclic matrix $S$ defined above, (-@eq-lax-pair) gives $\mathcal A_\pm[\pi\vec\phi;\lambda]=S\mathcal A_\pm[\vec\phi;\lambda]S^{-1}$. This constant conjugation preserves the spectral invariants of the bulk transport matrix and hence the local charges generated from them (@sec-conserved-charges). Their densities are invariant up to total derivatives, whose endpoint terms can be absorbed into the local defect contribution. Thus $\rho$ on the left and $\rho\pi^{-1}$ on the right multiply a charge of any fixed spin by the same number. For spin $\pm2$, the cubic term fixes that number to $-1$: $A(\vec u,\vec u,\vec u)=2\sum_k(\vec\mu_k\cdot\vec u)^3$ is invariant under $\pi$ and changes sign under $\rho$. Hence the type-I$_-$ defect with $\sigma$ keeps the charge of spin $s$, with a local defect contribution, exactly when the one with $1/\sigma$ keeps the charge of spin $-s$. If it kept $Q_{+2}$ and lost $Q_{-2}$ for every $\sigma$, it would keep $Q_{-2}$ at $1/\sigma$. The composite map also exchanges the two halves of $\mathcal B_d$, sending $\sigma^{-1}g_j$ to $\sigma'f_{-j}$ with $\sigma'=1/\sigma$, which is why the velocities in $\mathcal B_{+2}$ and in $\mathcal B_{-2}$ multiply different halves in (3). The cyclic conjugation of the bulk Lax pair, the time reversal, the composite map on soliton solutions and the transformation of $A$ are checked in `code/defect_ar_partners.py`.

So the two types are not distinguished by which spin-$\pm2$ charge survives. They differ in the $\lambda$-dependence of $\tilde L$, in the Borel subalgebra of the quantum group that their quantum transmission matrices intertwine (@prp-two-borels), and, for sine-Gordon, in the direction of soliton conversion: type I$_-$ converts solitons faster than the defect, type I$_+$ slower ones (@prp-sg-delay). This is why the book names the types by their Borel subalgebra. Classically the two types are related by symmetries of the bulk applied differently on the two sides of the defect (@prp-dc-types), as they are for sine-Gordon theory, where part (3) of @prp-two-borels gives the quantum form of the relation.

**The spin-$\pm3$ charges of sine-Gordon theory.** For $a_1^{(1)}$ the first charges beyond energy and momentum have spin $\pm3$, and their defect contributions have a closed form. Use the conventions of @sec-defect-sine-gordon, with $\beta=\beta_{\rm SG}$ and the type-I$_-$ conditions (-@eq-sg-defect-conditions), and write $c_\pm=\cos\frac\beta2(\phi\pm\psi)$ at $x=0$. Then $c_+$ is the half of $\mathcal B_d$ (-@eq-sg-defect-potential) with $\sigma$ and $c_-$ the half with $\sigma^{-1}$. In the convention of this part, in which $E+P$ has spin $+1$, a density built from $\partial_+$ has negative spin.

::: {#prp-sg-spin-three}
## The spin-$\pm3$ charges of the sine-Gordon defect
**[Theorem]** Let
$$
q_{\mp3}(\phi)=\frac{\beta^2}{8m_0^3}\Big[(\partial_\pm^2\phi)^2-\frac{\beta^2}4(\partial_\pm\phi)^4+m_0^2\cos(\beta\phi)\,(\partial_\pm\phi)^2\Big],
$$
which for the upper sign is $\beta^2/8m_0^3$ times the density $T_4-\mathcal X_2$ of (-@eq-spin3-current) continued to sine-Gordon theory, and let
$$
\mathcal D_{-3}=\frac{\sigma\beta^2}{2m_0^2}\,c_+\,\partial_+\phi\,\partial_+\psi+\sigma^3\Big(c_+-\frac23c_+^3\Big),\qquad
\mathcal D_{+3}=-\frac{\beta^2}{2m_0^2\sigma}\,c_-\,\partial_-\phi\,\partial_-\psi+\frac1{\sigma^3}\Big(c_--\frac23c_-^3\Big)
$$ {#eq-dc-spin-three}
at $x=0$. Then
$$
Q_{\mp3}=\int_{-\infty}^0q_{\mp3}(\phi)\,dx+\int_0^\infty q_{\mp3}(\psi)\,dx+\mathcal D_{\mp3}
$$
are conserved. A soliton of rapidity $\theta$ has $Q_{\mp3}=-\frac23e^{\mp3\theta}$, while $\frac{\beta^2}{8m_0}(E\mp P)=e^{\mp\theta}$. The static jump $(\phi,\psi)=(0,2\pi/\beta)$ has $\mathcal D_{\mp3}=-\frac13\sigma^{\pm3}$ and the vacuum $(0,0)$ has $\mathcal D_{\mp3}=\frac13\sigma^{\pm3}$. So, relative to the vacuum, the jump stores $-\frac23\sigma^{\pm3}=-\frac23e^{\mp3\theta_d}$, the spin-$\mp3$ charge of a soliton of rapidity $\theta_d$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By (-@eq-spin3-current) with $\beta^2\to-\beta^2$, $q_{-3}$ is conserved with the current $j_{-3}=\frac{\beta^2}{8m_0^3}\big[m_0^2\cos(\beta\phi)(\partial_+\phi)^2-(\partial_+^2\phi)^2+\frac{\beta^2}4(\partial_+\phi)^4\big]$, so the bulk part of $Q_{-3}$ changes by $j_{-3}(\psi)-j_{-3}(\phi)$ at $x=0$. There the defect conditions give $\partial_x\phi$ and $\partial_x\psi$ in terms of the defect values and their time derivatives, their time derivatives give $\partial_t\partial_x\phi$ and $\partial_t\partial_x\psi$, and the field equations give $\partial_x^2\phi$ and $\partial_x^2\psi$. The flux becomes a function of $\phi$, $\psi$ and their first two time derivatives at $x=0$, and it equals $-\frac d{dt}\mathcal D_{-3}$ identically. The terms quadratic in $\partial_t^2\phi$, $\partial_t^2\psi$ cancel because $\partial_+=2\partial_t-\partial_-$, so that $\partial_+^2(\phi-\psi)$ is fixed by the time derivative of the light-cone condition for $\partial_+(\phi-\psi)$ and by the field equations. The lower sign is the same computation with $\partial_-$ and the condition for $\partial_-(\phi+\psi)$. We checked both identities exactly, with $\sigma$ symbolic. With $\mathcal D_{\mp3}$ evaluated at $1.1\sigma$ they fail, and with $c_+$ replaced by $\cos\frac{0.9\beta}2(\phi+\psi)$ in $\mathcal B_d$ the flux is not the time derivative of any local function, because its Euler operator in $t$ does not vanish. The soliton charges were computed by quadrature for several $\theta$. Along exact passages of a soliton with $\theta<\theta_d$ and $\theta>\theta_d$, and along the absorption at $\theta=\theta_d$, $Q_{\mp3}$ are constant to $10^{-13}$ and take the values that the last two statements predict; without $\mathcal D_{\mp3}$ they are not constant (`code/defect_sg_spin3.py`).
:::

As for $E\mp P$ in @prp-sg-defect-momentum, $\mathcal D_{-3}$ contains only the half $c_+$ of the defect potential, with $\sigma$, and $\mathcal D_{+3}$ only the half $c_-$, with $\sigma^{-1}$. A jump of $2\pi/\beta$ stores not only the energy and momentum of a soliton of rapidity $\theta_d$ but also its spin-$\pm3$ charges. With the constants in (-@eq-dc-spin-three), $\mathcal D_{\mp3}$ is half the charge of a soliton of rapidity $\theta_d$ at the odd jump and half that of rapidity $\theta_d+i\pi$ at the vacuum, the pattern that part 1 of @prp-half-soliton finds for the energy and momentum after a constant is added (same script). The proposition makes part (2) of @prp-spin-two explicit for $a_1^{(1)}$ at the first spin beyond 1. Bowcock, Corrigan and Zambon [-@bcz2004, eqs. (2.4)–(2.5)] required only the sum $Q_3+Q_{-3}$, the "energy-like" combination, to be conserved, and did not write its defect term. Caudrelier [-@caudrelier2008, eq. (3.28)] derived the defect term of the spin-3 charge from the defect matrix, for sine-Gordon theory in light-cone coordinates with the defect on a line of constant light-cone coordinate. On his defect condition [@caudrelier2008, eq. (3.29)] his term is a constant multiple of $\mathcal D_{-3}$ (same script).

## The defect monodromy and the classical r-matrix {#sec-defect-r-matrix}

The transport matrix $T(x_+,x_-;\lambda)$ of @sec-sklyanin, with $\partial_{x_+}T=-a_x(x_+)T$, carries $\Psi$ from $x_-$ to $x_+$. A solution on the whole line crosses the defect by $\Psi_\psi=L_d^{-1}\Psi_\phi$, so the **defect monodromy** is

$$
\mathcal T_d(\lambda)=T_+(\lambda)\,L_d(\lambda)^{-1}\,T_-(\lambda),\qquad\tau_d(\lambda)=\operatorname{tr}\mathcal T_d(\lambda),
$$ {#eq-defect-monodromy}

with $T_+=T^\psi(x_+,0)$ and $T_-=T^\phi(0,x_-)$. The evolution equation of $L_d^{-1}$, $\partial_tL_d^{-1}=L_d^{-1}a_t(\vec\phi)-a_t(\vec\psi)L_d^{-1}$, is exactly what makes the boundary terms at $x=0$ cancel, and with fields that decay at $x_\pm\to\pm\infty$ the generating function $\tau_d(\lambda)$ is conserved [@bcz2004b, eq. (5.1)]. (They write the inverse matrix, transporting from right to left.)

**The Poisson structure of the defect values.** Integrability in the sense of Liouville also needs the charges to Poisson-commute. The defect term in (-@eq-defect-action) is first order in time derivatives, so it is a symplectic potential for the defect values $\vec z=(\vec\phi(0),\vec\psi(0))$, regarded as independent coordinates. Up to a total time derivative it equals $\frac12\vec z\cdot K\partial_t\vec z$ with

$$
K=\begin{pmatrix}E&\mathsf D\\-\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}&E\end{pmatrix},\qquad\{z_I,z_J\}=(K^{-1})_{IJ},
$$ {#eq-dc-defect-bracket}

in the convention $\{\phi_a(x),\pi_b(y)\}=\delta_{ab}\delta(x-y)$ of the bulk. For sine-Gordon $\{\phi(0),\psi(0)\}=-1$ for type I$_-$ and $+1$ for type I$_+$. Treating the defect term as a pair of second-class constraints, as Corrigan and Zambon [-@cz2009b, Sec. 6] do for sine-Gordon theory, gives the same Dirac bracket (by hand). The defect matrix is built from exponentials of linear functions of $\vec z$, so its bracket with itself is quadratic in $L_d$, and the question is whether it has the Sklyanin form.

::: {#prp-defect-involution}
## Poisson algebra of the defect matrix
**[Theorem for $a_1^{(1)}$; Numerical for $a_2^{(1)}$–$a_4^{(1)}$]** Give the defect values the bracket (-@eq-dc-defect-bracket), as independent coordinates Poisson-commuting with the bulk fields. Then, for $a_r^{(1)}$, both types and both couplings,
$$
\{L_d(\lambda_1)\overset\otimes,L_d(\lambda_2)\}=\Big[r\Big(\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}\Big),\,L_d(\lambda_1)\otimes L_d(\lambda_2)\Big],
$$
with the r-matrix $r(z)$ of @prp-sklyanin ($\beta^2\to b^2$) and coefficient exactly 1. For $a_1^{(1)}$ and $\lambda_1^2\ne\lambda_2^2$ this relation determines $r(z)$ up to a multiple of the identity, which drops out of the commutator. The bulk transport matrices satisfy $\{T(\lambda_1)\overset\otimes,T(\lambda_2)\}=-[r,T(\lambda_1)\otimes T(\lambda_2)]$ (@prp-sklyanin), so $L_d^{-1}$, and with it $\mathcal T_d$, satisfies the same quadratic relation as $T$, and $\{\tau_d(\lambda_1),\tau_d(\lambda_2)\}=0$. For $a_r^{(1)}$ with $r\ge2$ the bracket of $L_d$ is the numerical part; the step from it to involution is exact.
:::

::: {.proof}
*The case $a_1^{(1)}$.* In the two-dimensional representation of @exr-dc-lax, with $H=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)/\sqrt2$, $\sigma_x=E_{\vec\alpha}+E_{-\vec\alpha}$ and $\Pi=E_{\vec\alpha}\otimes E_{-\vec\alpha}+E_{-\vec\alpha}\otimes E_{\vec\alpha}$, the type-I$_-$ defect matrix is $L_d(\lambda)=\mathsf J+\frac\sigma\lambda\mathsf O$ with $\mathsf J=e^{bH(\phi-\psi)/2}$ and $\mathsf O=e^{-bH(\phi+\psi)/2}\sigma_x$. Let $\epsilon=\{\phi(0),\psi(0)\}$. Then $\{\phi-\psi,\phi+\psi\}=2\epsilon$, while $\phi-\psi$ and $\phi+\psi$ each have zero bracket with themselves, and the chain rule gives, in the notation of @prp-sklyanin,
$$
\{\overset1{\mathsf J},\overset2{\mathsf O}\}=\kappa\,H\otimes H\,X,\qquad\{\overset1{\mathsf O},\overset2{\mathsf J}\}=-\kappa\,H\otimes H\,X',\qquad\{\overset1{\mathsf J},\overset2{\mathsf J}\}=\{\overset1{\mathsf O},\overset2{\mathsf O}\}=0,
$$
with $\kappa=-b^2\epsilon/2$, $X=\mathsf J\otimes\mathsf O$ and $X'=\mathsf O\otimes\mathsf J$. Hence $\{L_d(\lambda_1)\overset\otimes,L_d(\lambda_2)\}=\kappa\sigma\,H\otimes H\,(X/\lambda_2-X'/\lambda_1)$. On the other side take $r=A\,H\otimes H+G\,\Pi$. Both $H\otimes H$ and $\Pi$ commute with $H\otimes1+1\otimes H$ and with $\sigma_x\otimes\sigma_x$, hence with $\mathsf J\otimes\mathsf J$ and $\mathsf O\otimes\mathsf O$. Since $\sigma_x$ anticommutes with $H$, $[H\otimes H,X]=2\,H\otimes H\,X$, and a short computation with $E_{\pm\vec\alpha}E_{\mp\vec\alpha}=\frac12\pm\frac1{\sqrt2}H$ gives $[\Pi,X]=-2\,H\otimes H\,X'$; both also hold with $X$ and $X'$ exchanged. So
$$
\big[r,L_d(\lambda_1)\otimes L_d(\lambda_2)\big]=2\sigma\,H\otimes H\Big[\Big(\frac A{\lambda_2}-\frac G{\lambda_1}\Big)X+\Big(\frac A{\lambda_1}-\frac G{\lambda_2}\Big)X'\Big].
$$
The matrices $H\otimes H\,X$ and $H\otimes H\,X'$ are linearly independent, so with $z=\lambda_1/\lambda_2$ the relation holds exactly when $2A-2G/z=\kappa$ and $2A-2Gz=-\kappa$. The unique solution is
$$
r(z)=\frac\kappa{2(z^2-1)}\Big[(z^2+1)\,H\otimes H+2z\,\Pi\Big],
$$
which is $-\epsilon$ times the r-matrix of @prp-sklyanin for $h=2$. The type-I$_-$ bracket $\epsilon=-1$ gives it with coefficient exactly 1. The ansatz for $r$ is not needed. Two solutions differ by a matrix $\rho$ that commutes with $L_d(\lambda_1)\otimes L_d(\lambda_2)$ for all defect values, hence with the coefficient of each exponential of $\phi$ and $\psi$ separately. Let $v_\pm$ be the eigenvectors of $H$. The coefficients of $e^{\pm b(\phi-\psi)/\sqrt2}$ and $e^{\pm b(\phi+\psi)/\sqrt2}$ generate all matrices on the span of $v_+\otimes v_+$ and $v_-\otimes v_-$, and vanish on the span $W$ of $v_+\otimes v_-$ and $v_-\otimes v_+$. So $\rho$ is a multiple $\nu$ of the identity on the first span and maps $W$ to itself. In the basis $v_+\otimes v_-$, $v_-\otimes v_+$ of $W$, the coefficients of $e^{\mp b\psi/\sqrt2}$ are $\sigma\,v_\pm\otimes v_\pm$ times the row vectors $(1/\lambda_2,1/\lambda_1)$ and $(1/\lambda_1,1/\lambda_2)$ respectively, so these row vectors are left eigenvectors of $\rho|_W$ with eigenvalue $\nu$. For $\lambda_1^2\ne\lambda_2^2$ they are independent, and $\rho=\nu$. For type I$_+$, $L_d^{\rm I_+}(\phi,\psi)\,\sigma_x=\frac\lambda\sigma L_d^{\rm I_-}(\phi,-\psi)$, and the type-I$_+$ bracket $\epsilon=+1$ gives $\{\phi,-\psi\}=-1$; the scalar factor, and $\sigma_x\otimes\sigma_x$, which commutes with $r$, leave the relation unchanged. Nothing depends on whether $b$ is real or imaginary. All steps, the uniqueness without an ansatz, and the failure for $\epsilon=+1$ and at $\lambda_2=\pm\lambda_1$ are checked in `code/defect_sklyanin_a1.py`, which also derives the bracket of $a_x$ in (b) of @prp-sklyanin for $a_1^{(1)}$, the input of the bulk relation.

*The numerical check.* The bracket of $L_d$ follows from (-@eq-dc-defect-bracket) by the chain rule. We compared it with $[r,L_d\otimes L_d]$ for $a_1,\dots,a_4$, both types, both couplings and real and complex $\lambda_{1,2}$: the relative residual is $10^{-15}$ and the coefficient is $1$ to $10^{-15}$. A non-integrable $\mathsf D$ leaves a residual of 0.2 (`code/defect_lax_rmatrix.py`). For the bulk sign, the transport matrix over one lattice site of length $\Delta$, $T=e^{-\Delta a_x}$ with $\{\phi_a,\pi_b\}=\delta_{ab}/\Delta$, satisfies $\{T\overset\otimes,T\}=c\,[r,T\otimes T]$ with $c=-1+O(\Delta)$ (same script). If $\{L_1,L_2\}=[r,L_1L_2]$ then $\{L_1^{-1},L_2^{-1}\}=-[r,L_1^{-1}L_2^{-1}]$, so all three factors of $\mathcal T_d$ obey the same quadratic algebra, and their product does too, since the factors Poisson-commute. Then $\{\operatorname{tr}\mathcal T_d(\lambda_1),\operatorname{tr}\mathcal T_d(\lambda_2)\}=\mp\operatorname{tr}_{12}[r,\mathcal T_{d1}\mathcal T_{d2}]=0$. We checked the involution with random $T_\pm$ satisfying the bulk relation and the computed bracket of $L_d^{-1}$, to $10^{-14}$; it fails if $L_d$ replaces $L_d^{-1}$ in (-@eq-defect-monodromy), or if the defect bracket has the wrong sign (same script).
:::

The normalization is the point. The defect term was fixed in @sec-defect-momentum by momentum conservation, which knows nothing about Poisson brackets. That its symplectic form makes $L_d$ a classical $L$-operator for exactly the bulk r-matrix, with coefficient 1 and the right sign, is a strong consistency check, and it is the classical shadow of the quantum statement that the transmission matrix is an $L$-operator of a Borel subalgebra (@sec-t-intertwiner). For $a_1^{(1)}$ the proof shows more. The defect matrix alone fixes the r-matrix, up to the factor $-\epsilon$ and a multiple of the identity, and agreement with the bulk r-matrix selects $\epsilon=-1$, which is the bracket that the kinetic term gives. Habibullin and Kundu [-@habibullin_kundu2008, eqs. (5.73)–(5.81)] met the same algebraic structure, Cartan exponentials on the diagonal and an off-diagonal partner with a constant bracket, in the lattice defect operator of their regularization. There the bracket comes from canonical momenta at the lattice site of the defect, and the dependence on them drops out in the continuum limit [@habibullin_kundu2008, Sec. 5.2]. Since the brackets of the linear functions $\vec\alpha_j\cdot\vec w$ and $\vec\phi-\vec\psi$ are constants, their exponentials form a Poisson algebra of Weyl type, the classical limit of the $q$-Weyl algebras behind the $q$-oscillator representations of the quantum theory.

**What the proposition does not settle.** The proposition concerns a finite-dimensional Poisson algebra. The assumption that the defect values, which are the endpoint values of the bulk fields, can be treated as independent coordinates that Poisson-commute with the bulk fields is the delicate step. The equal-time bracket of the field theory does not restrict to the boundary values of fields in a well-defined way, and the direct use of the r-matrix is hindered by divergences at the defect [@caudrelier2015, Sec. 1]. There are two ways around this. Habibullin and Kundu [-@habibullin_kundu2008] regularized the sine-Gordon defect on a lattice and derived its classical and quantum r-matrix structure and all its charges. Avan and Doikou [-@avan_doikou2012a; -@avan_doikou2012b] postulated a defect matrix satisfying the quadratic algebra, regarded its entries as independent degrees of freedom, and imposed "sewing conditions" with the bulk as constraints with Dirac brackets; they reported discrepancies with the charges of the Lagrangian approach. Doikou [-@doikou2014] extended the construction to $\mathfrak{gl}_N$ type-I defects in spin chains. Caudrelier [-@caudrelier2008; -@caudrelier2015] and Caudrelier and Kundu [-@caudrelier_kundu2015] resolved the tension differently. In a second, "time-like" Poisson bracket, in which $x$ plays the role of time, the sine-Gordon model is Hamiltonian with the same r-matrix, and the defect conditions are a canonical transformation. In the book's conventions this is immediate from the action: with $G[\vec\phi,\vec\psi]=\int dt\,\big[\frac12\vec\phi\cdot E\vec\phi_t+\vec\phi\cdot\mathsf D\vec\psi_t+\frac12\vec\psi\cdot E\vec\psi_t-\mathcal B_d\big]$, the conditions (-@eq-defect-conditions) read $\partial_x\vec\phi=\delta G/\delta\vec\phi(0,t)$ and $\partial_x\vec\psi=-\delta G/\delta\vec\psi(0,t)$, so the map from $(\vec\phi,-\partial_x\vec\phi)$ to $(\vec\psi,-\partial_x\vec\psi)$ on the line $x=0$ is generated by $-G$ [@caudrelier2015, Prop. 3.1]. Caudrelier [-@caudrelier2015, Sec. 3.3] then proved Liouville integrability of the sine-Gordon defect with the r-matrix in the time-like bracket. For $a_r^{(1)}$ the same steps should go through, but we have not carried them out.

**Comparison with a boundary.** The boundary generating function $\tau(\lambda)=\operatorname{tr}(K_+T(\lambda)K_-(1/\lambda)\sigma(T(1/\lambda)))$ of (-@eq-double-row) is built from one transport matrix and its image, and integrability requires the reflection equation (-@eq-classical-reflection) for the field-independent $K_\pm$. The defect generating function is built from two independent transport matrices and a field-dependent $L_d$, and integrability requires that $L_d$ itself be a representation of the bulk Poisson algebra. A defect pressed against a boundary therefore produces a field-dependent $K$-matrix, $K_+(\lambda)$ dressed by $L_d$, which is how the defect parameter becomes a boundary parameter in @sec-sg-breather-transmission and @sec-defect-boundary-fusion.

## Defect conditions as Bäcklund transformations {#sec-defect-backlund-an}

For sine-Gordon theory the defect conditions are a Bäcklund transformation frozen at $x=0$ (@sec-sg-defect-lagrangian). The same is true for $a_r^{(1)}$. Bowcock, Corrigan and Zambon asked when conditions of the form (-@eq-defect-conditions), imposed for all $x$, are compatible with Lorentz-invariant field equations on both sides. Cross-differentiating gives $\partial_x^2\Psi=M^2\partial_t^2\Psi+\dots$ with $\Psi=(\vec\phi,\vec\psi)$ and $M=\begin{pmatrix}E&\mathsf D\\\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}&-F\end{pmatrix}$, and decoupled Lorentz-invariant equations require $M^2=1$, a condition on the second derivatives of $\mathcal B_d$, and condition 3 of @prp-defect-momentum [@bcz2004b, eqs. (5.19)–(5.25)]. Solving these reproduces (-@eq-d-matrix) and (-@eq-defect-potential) [@bcz2004b, eqs. (5.26)–(5.43)]. We checked directly that for $r=1,\dots,4$, both types and both couplings, cross-differentiation of the conditions gives both field equations, and that a non-integrable $\mathsf D$ does not (`code/defect_classical_an.py`). Conversely, every defect that satisfies the three conditions of @prp-defect-momentum is a Bäcklund transformation when imposed for all $x$, and the light-cone form (-@eq-dc-lightcone) shows this in a few lines. Apply $\partial_-$ to its first equation and $\partial_+$ to its second. With $H_f$ and $H_g$ the matrices of second derivatives of $f$ and $g$, this gives $\partial_+\partial_-(\vec\phi-\vec\psi)=-2H_f\partial_-\vec\xi=-4H_f\nabla g$ and $\partial_+\partial_-\vec\xi=2H_g\partial_+(\vec\phi-\vec\psi)=-4H_g\nabla f$, so that $\partial_+\partial_-\vec\phi=-2(H_g\nabla f+\mathsf DH_f\nabla g)$. The gradient of $2\nabla f\cdot\nabla g=V(\vec\phi)-V(\vec\psi)$ with respect to $\vec\phi$ at fixed $\vec\psi$, with $\nabla_{\vec\phi}=\mathsf D\nabla_{\vec\xi}+\nabla_{\vec\eta}$, is $2(\mathsf DH_f\nabla g+H_g\nabla f)=\nabla V(\vec\phi)$. So $\partial_+\partial_-\vec\phi=-\nabla V(\vec\phi)$, and the same steps give $\partial_+\partial_-\vec\psi=-\nabla V(\vec\psi)$. In the components (-@eq-dc-components) the transformation reads

$$
\partial_+\big(\phi_k-\psi_k\big)=-\frac{m\sigma}b\big(f_k-f_{k-1}\big),\qquad\partial_-\big(\psi_k-\phi_{k+1}\big)=\frac m{b\sigma}\big(g_k-g_{k+1}\big),
$$

a Bäcklund transformation of the periodic two-dimensional Toda lattice $\partial_+\partial_-\phi_k=-\frac{m^2}b\big(e^{b(\phi_k-\phi_{k+1})}-e^{b(\phi_{k-1}-\phi_k)}\big)$, which is the field equation in components (`code/defect_ar_partners.py`). Write $\vec\psi=\mathfrak B_\sigma\vec\phi$ for this Bäcklund transformation. For $a_2^{(1)}$ it is the Bäcklund transformation of Fordy and Gibbons, as Corrigan and Zambon [-@cz2009b, Sec. 5] observed.

**The defect matrix is the gauge transformation.** Cross-differentiation shows that the unfrozen conditions are a Bäcklund transformation, and the defect matrix shows why. Imposed for all $x$, the conditions make $L_d$ intertwine the two Lax pairs in both light-cone directions, not only in time.

::: {#prp-dc-gauge}
## The defect matrix as a gauge transformation
**[Theorem]** Let $\vec\phi$ and $\vec\psi$ satisfy the defect conditions (-@eq-defect-conditions) of either type on an open region, and let $\mathcal A_\pm$ be the Lax pair (-@eq-lax-pair) with $\beta\to b$. Then, for all $\lambda$, the defect matrix (-@eq-defect-lax-matrix) satisfies
$$
\partial_\pm L_d=L_d\,\mathcal A_\pm(\vec\psi)-\mathcal A_\pm(\vec\phi)\,L_d .
$$ {#eq-dc-gauge}
For each type the $\partial_+$ and $\partial_-$ equations are equivalent to the two halves of its defect conditions in components, imposed for all $x$; for type I$_-$ these are the Bäcklund transformation above, and the proof displays both. Wherever $L_d$ is invertible, which fails only at finitely many $\lambda$, the curvature $[\partial_++\mathcal A_+,\partial_-+\mathcal A_-]$ of $\vec\psi$ is $L_d^{-1}$ times that of $\vec\phi$ times $L_d$. So $\vec\psi$ solves the field equation exactly when $\vec\phi$ does.
:::

::: {.proof}
For type I$_-$, in the components (-@eq-dc-components), $L_d$ has the diagonal entries $g_k^{1/2}=e^{b(\phi_k-\psi_k)/2}$, the entries $\frac\sigma\lambda f_j^{1/2}=\frac\sigma\lambda e^{b(\psi_j-\phi_{j+1})/2}$ in the positions $(j+1,j)$, and no others. With the matrix units $e_{jk}$, the Lax pair is $\mathcal A_+=\frac b2\operatorname{diag}(\partial_+\phi_k)+m\lambda\sum_je^{b(\phi_j-\phi_{j+1})/2}e_{j,j+1}$ and $\mathcal A_-=-\frac b2\operatorname{diag}(\partial_-\phi_k)-\frac m\lambda\sum_je^{b(\phi_j-\phi_{j+1})/2}e_{j+1,j}$. Compare powers of $\lambda$. In the $\partial_+$ equation, order $\lambda$ holds because $g_j^{1/2}e^{b(\psi_j-\psi_{j+1})/2}=e^{b(\phi_j-\phi_{j+1})/2}g_{j+1}^{1/2}$, and order $\lambda^{-1}$ holds identically. Order $\lambda^0$ is diagonal. Since $f_{k-1}^{1/2}e^{b(\psi_{k-1}-\psi_k)/2}=f_{k-1}g_k^{1/2}$ and $e^{b(\phi_k-\phi_{k+1})/2}f_k^{1/2}=f_kg_k^{1/2}$, it reads $\partial_+(\phi_k-\psi_k)=-\frac{m\sigma}b(f_k-f_{k-1})$. In the $\partial_-$ equation, order $\lambda^0$ holds identically, and order $\lambda^{-2}$ holds because $f_k^{1/2}e^{b(\psi_{k-1}-\psi_k)/2}=e^{b(\phi_k-\phi_{k+1})/2}f_{k-1}^{1/2}$. Order $\lambda^{-1}$ has entries only in the positions $(j+1,j)$. Since $e^{b(\phi_j-\phi_{j+1})/2}g_j^{1/2}=g_jf_j^{1/2}$ and $g_{j+1}^{1/2}e^{b(\psi_j-\psi_{j+1})/2}=g_{j+1}f_j^{1/2}$, it reads $\partial_-(\psi_j-\phi_{j+1})=\frac m{b\sigma}(g_j-g_{j+1})$. These are the two halves of the Bäcklund transformation.

For type I$_+$ put $\zeta=\lambda/\sigma$ and $c(\lambda)=1-\zeta^h$. Since $S^h=1$, $(1-\zeta S)\sum_{k=0}^{h-1}\zeta^kS^k=c(\lambda)$, and the scaled inverse $M=c(\lambda)L_d^{-1}$ has the diagonal entries $g_k^{1/2}$, the entries $-\zeta f_j^{1/2}$ in the positions $(j,j+1)$, and no others. Its determinant is $c(\lambda)$, so $\det L_d=c(\lambda)^{h-1}$. Away from the zeros of $c$, (-@eq-dc-gauge) is equivalent to $\partial_\pm M=M\mathcal A_\pm(\vec\phi)-\mathcal A_\pm(\vec\psi)M$. In the $\partial_+$ equation, order $\lambda^0$ holds identically, and order $\lambda^2$ holds because $f_j^{1/2}e^{b(\phi_{j+1}-\phi_{j+2})/2}=e^{b(\psi_j-\psi_{j+1})/2}f_{j+1}^{1/2}$. Order $\lambda$ has entries only in the positions $(j,j+1)$. Since $g_j^{1/2}e^{b(\phi_j-\phi_{j+1})/2}=g_jf_j^{1/2}$ and $e^{b(\psi_j-\psi_{j+1})/2}g_{j+1}^{1/2}=g_{j+1}f_j^{1/2}$, it reads $\partial_+(\psi_j-\phi_{j+1})=-\frac{m\sigma}b(g_j-g_{j+1})$. In the $\partial_-$ equation, order $\lambda$ holds identically, and order $\lambda^{-1}$ holds because $g_{j+1}^{1/2}e^{b(\phi_j-\phi_{j+1})/2}=e^{b(\psi_j-\psi_{j+1})/2}g_j^{1/2}$. Order $\lambda^0$ is diagonal. Since $f_k^{1/2}e^{b(\phi_k-\phi_{k+1})/2}=f_kg_k^{1/2}$ and $e^{b(\psi_{k-1}-\psi_k)/2}f_{k-1}^{1/2}=f_{k-1}g_k^{1/2}$, it reads $\partial_-(\phi_k-\psi_k)=\frac m{b\sigma}(f_k-f_{k-1})$. These are the two halves of the type-I$_+$ conditions in components. Both sides of (-@eq-dc-gauge) are Laurent polynomials in $\lambda$, so the equation holds for all $\lambda\ne0$, not only away from the zeros of $c$.

For either type, (-@eq-dc-gauge) says $\mathcal A_\pm(\vec\psi)=L_d^{-1}\mathcal A_\pm(\vec\phi)L_d+L_d^{-1}\partial_\pm L_d$, a gauge transformation, and a gauge transformation conjugates the curvature. For type I$_-$, $\det L_d=1-(-\sigma/\lambda)^h$. The curvature is a Laurent polynomial in $\lambda$, so if that of $\vec\phi$ vanishes, that of $\vec\psi$ vanishes for all $\lambda$, which by (-@eq-zero-curvature) is the field equation. The order-by-order computation was checked symbolically for $h=3,4$ for type I$_-$, and for $h=2,3,4$ and with six free field values for type I$_+$. Both equations (-@eq-dc-gauge), in the form of a $\partial_t$ and a $\partial_x$ equation with $\partial_x\vec\phi$, $\partial_x\vec\psi$ from the defect conditions, were checked at random points for $h=2,\dots,5$, both types and both couplings, to $10^{-12}$; they fail for $1.2\sigma$ in $L_d$ and for $0.6E$ in the conditions (`code/defect_ar_gauge.py`).
:::

The time component of (-@eq-dc-gauge), half the sum of its two equations, is the evolution equation (-@eq-defect-lax-matrix). At a defect only this component survives, because the conditions hold only at $x=0$ and fix no $x$-derivative of $L_d$. Frozen at a point, the gauge transformation becomes the matrix that glues the two linear problems. Bowcock, Corrigan and Zambon [-@bcz2004b, eq. (3.7)] imposed only the time equation and obtained the Bäcklund transformation by cross-differentiation [-@bcz2004b, Sec. 5.1]. For the equations of the AKNS scheme, sine-Gordon theory among them, Caudrelier [-@caudrelier2008, eqs. (1.12)–(1.13), (3.26)] required the defect matrix to satisfy both equations of the linear problem, at every $x$ and $t$.

**The delay is the Bianchi coefficient.** Send the soliton (-@eq-an-soliton) of species $a$ and rapidity $\theta$ through a type-I$_-$ defect at imaginary coupling, and look for $\vec\psi$ of the same form with $E\to z_aE$. The defect conditions hold for all $t$ exactly when

$$
z_a(\theta)=\frac{e^{-(\theta-\theta_d)}-ie^{i\pi a/h}}{e^{-(\theta-\theta_d)}-ie^{-i\pi a/h}}
=\frac{\mathsf a(\theta)+\varepsilon_a\,\mathsf a(\theta_d)}{\mathsf a(\theta)-\varepsilon_a^{-1}\mathsf a(\theta_d)},\qquad\mathsf a(\theta)=-e^{-\theta},\quad\varepsilon_a=e^{i\pi(2a-h)/2h},
$$ {#eq-dc-ar-delay}

which is [@cz2009a, eq. (4.10)], [@bcz2004b, eq. (6.2)] after $\theta\to-\theta$, and @cz2007 [eq. (2.20)] after $a\to h-a$, because their $\mathsf D$ is the book's $\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}$. The pair $(\vec\phi,\vec\psi)$ of full-line solutions satisfies the conditions not only at $x=0$ but at every $x$: it is a Bäcklund pair, $\vec\psi=\mathfrak B_\sigma\vec\phi$. So the delay is the factor by which $\mathfrak B_\sigma$ multiplies $E$, the $a_r$ version of the Bianchi coefficient of (-@eq-sgd-bianchi), and the second form of (-@eq-dc-ar-delay) displays it with the Bäcklund parameters $\mathsf a(\theta)$ of @prp-sg-backlund. For $h=2$, $\varepsilon_1=1$ and it reduces to $z_{\rm I_-}$ of (-@eq-sg-delay). For $h>2$ the coefficient is twisted by the phase $\varepsilon_a$, and $z_a$ is complex for real rapidities; the phase of $z_a$ is what moves the topological charge of a passing soliton along its cycle of charges (@prp-stored-charge). Two identities generalize those of @prp-half-soliton:

$$
z_a(\theta)\,z_{\bar a}(\theta)=\frac{\cosh(\theta-\theta_d)+\sin\frac{\pi a}h}{\cosh(\theta-\theta_d)-\sin\frac{\pi a}h},\qquad
z_{\bar a}(\bar\theta;\bar\theta_d)=\overline{z_a(\theta;\theta_d)},\qquad\bar a=h-a.
$$

For $h=2$ the first is $z^2=\coth^2\frac{\theta-\theta_d}2=1/A_{11}$. For self-conjugate solitons, $a=h/2$, $z_{h/2}=-\coth\frac{\theta-\theta_d}2$ is the sine-Gordon delay, with the sign that converts solitons faster than the defect. We checked (-@eq-dc-ar-delay) by root-finding and at $x=0$, $-0.7$ and $1.3$ for $a_2^{(1)}$ (species 1 and 2), the self-conjugate soliton of $a_3^{(1)}$ and $a_1^{(1)}$, together with the dictionary to the three sources and the two identities (`code/defect_classical_an.py`). @sec-defect-solitons develops the consequences: the selection rule for the topological charge (@prp-stored-charge), the absence of absorption at real rapidity except for self-conjugate solitons, unless the defect carries a charged jump (@prp-ds-absorption), and multi-soliton transmission.

## Type-II defects in affine Toda theory {#sec-type-two-atft}

@prp-ar-only leaves every theory except $a_r^{(1)}$ without a type-I defect. Corrigan and Zambon [-@cz2009b] found a way out for the Tzitzéica theory $a_2^{(2)}$ by giving the defect a degree of freedom $\Lambda(t)$ of its own. For one field component the defect term is

$$
\Big[\tfrac12(\phi\,\partial_t\psi-\psi\,\partial_t\phi)+\Lambda\,\partial_t(\phi-\psi)-(\phi-\psi)\,\partial_t\Lambda-\mathcal D(\phi,\psi,\Lambda)\Big]_{x=0},
$$ {#eq-dc-type-two}

and the defect conditions are $\partial_x\phi=\partial_t\psi-2\partial_t\Lambda-\partial_\phi\mathcal D$, $\partial_x\psi=\partial_t\phi-2\partial_t\Lambda+\partial_\psi\mathcal D$ and $\partial_t\phi-\partial_t\psi=\frac12\partial_\Lambda\mathcal D$ [@cz2009b, eqs. (2.1)–(2.4)]. As for type I, $E+\mathcal D$ is conserved for every $\mathcal D$. With $p=\frac12(\phi+\psi)$ and $q=\frac12(\phi-\psi)$, a modified momentum exists exactly when $\mathcal D=f(q,p-\Lambda)+g(q,\Lambda)$ with

$$
\tfrac12\big(\partial_qf\,\partial_\Lambda g-\partial_\Lambda f\,\partial_qg\big)=V(\phi)-V(\psi),
$$

and then $P+g-f$ is conserved [@cz2009b, eqs. (2.10)–(2.12)]. The left-hand side is the Poisson bracket of $f$ and $g$ with $\Lambda$ and $-2q$ as conjugate variables. This condition replaces condition 3 of @prp-defect-momentum. It is still strong, since all dependence on $\Lambda$ must cancel, but it admits the Tzitzéica potential, which condition 3 excludes [@cz2009b, Sec. 2].

::: {#prp-type-ii-momentum}
## Energy and momentum of type-II defects
**[Established; numerically checked for sine-Gordon and Tzitzéica]** For the sine-Gordon defect [@cz2009b, eq. (3.2)] and the Tzitzéica defect [@cz2009b, eq. (3.7)], $E+\mathcal D$ and $P+g-f$ are conserved, and a soliton passes with a pure delay. For sine-Gordon the delay is $\coth\frac{\theta-\theta_d-\tau}2\coth\frac{\theta-\theta_d+\tau}2$ or its inverse, depending on the sector of $\Lambda$; for Tzitzéica it is one of three delays whose product is 1.
:::

::: {.proof}
The conservation laws were checked at random complex points along the defect conditions, and the solitons by solving the two conditions without $\partial_t\Lambda$ for $e^{\hat\lambda}$ at each time and checking the third with a numerical derivative, to $10^{-7}$ (`code/defect_classical_an.py`), in the variables described next.
:::

**Sine-Gordon.** In the rescaled variables of Corrigan and Zambon, $\hat p=\beta_{\rm SG}p$, $\hat q=\beta_{\rm SG}q$, $\hat\lambda=\beta_{\rm SG}\Lambda$ and $\hat x=m_0x/\sqrt2$ for sinh-Gordon, the defect potential is $\mathcal D=\frac{m_0}{\sqrt2\,\beta_{\rm SG}^2}(f+g)$ with

$$
f=\frac1{\hat\sigma}\Big[2e^{\hat p-\hat\lambda}+e^{-\hat p+\hat\lambda}\big(e^{\hat q}+e^{-\hat q}+2\cosh2\tau\big)\Big],\qquad
g=\hat\sigma\Big[e^{\hat\lambda}\big(e^{\hat q}+e^{-\hat q}+2\cosh2\tau\big)+2e^{-\hat\lambda}\Big],
$$

and $\hat\sigma=e^{\theta_d}$ (their $\sigma=e^\eta$); sine-Gordon follows by $\beta_{\rm SG}\to i\beta_{\rm SG}$. The two parameters are the defect rapidity $\theta_d$ and $\tau$. With no jump, the vacuum has $e^{2\hat\lambda}=1/(2\cosh^2\tau)$ [@cz2009b, eq. (3.4)], and the two square roots give two sectors. If $e^{\hat\lambda}\to+1/(\sqrt2\cosh\tau)$ before the soliton arrives, the delay is

$$
z=\coth\frac{\theta-\theta_d-\tau}2\,\coth\frac{\theta-\theta_d+\tau}2=z_{\rm I_-}(\theta;\theta_d+\tau)\,z_{\rm I_-}(\theta;\theta_d-\tau),
$$

the delay of two type-I$_-$ defects at rapidities $\theta_d\pm\tau$ without jumps. If $e^{\hat\lambda}\to-1/(\sqrt2\cosh\tau)$, that is $\hat\lambda\to\hat\lambda+i\pi$, the delay is its inverse, $\tanh\frac{\theta-\theta_d-\tau}2\tanh\frac{\theta-\theta_d+\tau}2$, the product of two odd-sector delays $z_{\rm odd}=-\tanh\frac{\theta-\theta_d}2$ of @sec-sg-defect-solitons. This is the sector that Corrigan and Zambon [-@cz2009b, eq. (4.3)] call $z_1$. In that sector $e^{\hat\lambda}=-\frac1{\sqrt2\cosh\tau}\,\frac{(1+E_0)(1+zE_0)}{(1-\rho E_0)(1-\tilde\rho E_0)}$ with $E_0=E(0,t)$, $\rho=\tanh\frac{\theta-\theta_d+\tau}2$, $\tilde\rho=\tanh\frac{\theta-\theta_d-\tau}2$; their (4.4) has the opposite overall sign and $+\rho$, $+\tilde\rho$ in the denominator, and does not satisfy the defect conditions. The type-II defect is the fused pair of two type-I defects (@sec-type-two), and $\hat\lambda$ remembers the field between them.

**Tzitzéica.** In the book's normalization the $a_2^{(2)}$ theory has roots $\sqrt2$ (long, label 1) and $-1/\sqrt2$ (short, label 2), so $V_{\rm real}=\frac{m^2}{\beta^2}\big(e^{\sqrt2\beta\phi}+2e^{-\beta\phi/\sqrt2}-3\big)$ and the particle has mass$^2$ $3m^2$. Corrigan and Zambon's field is $u=\beta\phi/\sqrt2=\beta_{\rm lit}\phi$, with the coupling $\beta_{\rm lit}^2=\beta^2/2$ of the normalization in which the long root has length$^2$ 4 (@sec-conventions), and $\hat x=mx/\sqrt2$. Their defect potential is $\mathcal D=\frac{\sqrt2m}{\beta^2}(f+g)$ with

$$
f=\frac1{\hat\sigma}\Big[e^{2\hat p-2\hat\lambda}+e^{-\hat p+\hat\lambda}\big(e^{\hat q}+e^{-\hat q}\big)\Big],\qquad
g=\frac{\hat\sigma}2\Big[8e^{-\hat\lambda}+e^{2\hat\lambda}\big(e^{\hat q}+e^{-\hat q}\big)^2\Big],
$$

where $\hat p$, $\hat q$, $\hat\lambda$ are $\beta_{\rm lit}$ times $p$, $q$, $\Lambda$, and the factor $1/\hat\sigma$ multiplies both terms of $f$, as the defect conditions [@cz2009b, eq. (4.6)] and the momentum condition require. There is one parameter, and with $e^{\theta_d}=\sqrt2\hat\sigma$ the three delays are

$$
z_1=\coth\Big(\frac{\theta-\theta_d}2-\frac{i\pi}{12}\Big)\coth\Big(\frac{\theta-\theta_d}2+\frac{i\pi}{12}\Big),\qquad
z_{2,3}=\coth\Big(\frac{\theta-\theta_d}2\mp\frac{i\pi}4\Big)\tanh\Big(\frac{\theta-\theta_d}2\pm\frac{i\pi}{12}\Big),
$$

with $z_1z_2z_3=1$ and $z_3=\bar z_2$ for real rapidities [@cz2009b, eqs. (4.9)–(4.11)]. The sector is fixed by the asymptotic value of $e^{\hat\lambda}$, which is $1$, $e^{-2\pi i/3}$ and $e^{2\pi i/3}$ respectively. (Their (4.11) lists $z_3$ under the name $z_2$; the set of delays is unaffected.) These were the first integrable defects of a theory outside $a_r^{(1)}$. Corrigan and Zambon [-@cz2009b, Sec. 5] also obtained the Tzitzéica conditions by folding two "squeezed" $a_2^{(1)}$ defects, of opposite rotations, gave the type-II defects of $a_n^{(1)}$ as fused pairs of the two rotations [-@cz2011, eq. (2.6)], and computed the Tzitzéica transmission matrix [-@cz2011, Sec. 3], which @sec-a22-transmission takes up.

**Beyond.** Bristow and Bowcock [-@bristow_bowcock2017, Sec. 4] found momentum-conserving type-II defects for $a_n^{(1)}$, $b_n^{(1)}$, $c_n^{(1)}$ and $d_n^{(1)}$; their potentials (4.19), (4.23), (4.27), (4.30) identify these as the untwisted algebras, with Kac labels $1,1,2,\dots,2,1,1$ for $d_n^{(1)}$ and $1,2,\dots,2,1$ for $c_n^{(1)}$. Their $a_n^{(1)}$ defect is the fused pair of two type-I defects. They computed soliton delays through the $d_4^{(1)}$ defect, and Bristow [-@bristow2017, Secs. 3.3–3.4] constructed defect Lax matrices for the Tzitzéica and $d_4^{(1)}$ defects. We know of no defect for $e_6^{(1)}$, $e_7^{(1)}$ and $e_8^{(1)}$. We have not checked these results.

## Folding defects {#sec-defect-folding}

Folding gives non-simply-laced theories from simply-laced ones (@sec-affine-folding), and Robertson [-@robertson2014a] applied it to defects. A type-I defect of $a_r^{(1)}$ cannot be folded directly. The reflection of the diagram that folding uses maps $\pi$ to $\pi^{-1}$, hence $\mathsf D$ to $\mathsf D^{\mathsf T}$, so it maps a defect to its mirror image. A fused pair of a defect and its mirror image, a type-II defect of $a_r^{(1)}$ [@cz2011], is invariant, and its folding gives defects of three series:

- $a_{2n-1}^{(1)}\to c_n^{(1)}$, by the reflection that fixes nodes $0$ and $n$, the canonical folding of @tbl-foldings;
- $a_{2n}^{(1)}\to a_{2n}^{(2)}$, by the reflection $j\to-j$ that fixes node $0$, the first construction of @sec-affine-folding;
- $a_{2n-1}^{(1)}\to d_n^{(2)}$, by the fixed-point-free reflection $j\to1-j$, whose orbits $\{0,1\}$ and $\{n,n+1\}$ consist of adjacent roots and give the short end nodes. This parent is not the one in @tbl-foldings ($d_{n+1}^{(1)}$); the folded roots must be rescaled by $\sqrt2$, and space and time by $1/\sqrt2$, to reach the standard normalization [@robertson2014a, Sec. 2].

Momentum conservation in the folded theory forces the two parameters of the pair to be equal up to sign. Opposite signs give no defect at all, the second defect annihilating the first; equal signs give a genuine defect, through which folded solitons pass with a delay [@robertson2014a, Sec. 3]. For $c_2^{(1)}$ the result agrees with the defect found by Bristow and Bowcock directly. These defects are not type I, consistent with @prp-ar-only, and Robertson notes that they need not be the only ones. The folding of solitons is the same as on the half-line (@sec-images-cn), where $c_n$ solitons are invariant $a_{2n-1}$ solitons. In a sequel Robertson [-@robertson2014b] introduced fusing rules for $a_r^{(1)}$ defects, classically and quantum mechanically, and used them to build a new $a_3^{(1)}$ transmission matrix. We have not re-derived these results.

**Linear waves see the condition.** Write $x=\sigma e^\theta=e^{\theta-\theta_d}$ and $\gamma=\gamma_k$. The linear factors (-@eq-an-linear-transmission) are $\mathbb T^{\rm cl}_k=(1+xe^{i\gamma})/(1+xe^{-i\gamma})$ and, since $\gamma_{h-k}=\pi-\gamma_k$, $\mathbb T^{\rm cl}_{h-k}=(1-xe^{-i\gamma})/(1-xe^{i\gamma})$. The reflection maps the mode of particle $k$ to that of particle $h-k$, so the mirror image transmits particle $k$ with $\mathbb T^{\rm cl}_{h-k}$, as it delays solitons (@exr-dc-d-matrix). A defect with parameter $\sigma_1$ next to a mirror image with $\sigma_2$ therefore transmits particle $k$ with $\mathbb T^{\rm cl}_k(\sigma_1)\mathbb T^{\rm cl}_{h-k}(\sigma_2)$ and particle $h-k$ with $\mathbb T^{\rm cl}_{h-k}(\sigma_1)\mathbb T^{\rm cl}_k(\sigma_2)$. A wave that is invariant under the reflection stays invariant only if the two agree for every $\theta$, that is, if
$$
\frac{\mathbb T^{\rm cl}_k}{\mathbb T^{\rm cl}_{h-k}}=\frac{1-x^2e^{2i\gamma}}{1-x^2e^{-2i\gamma}}
$$
takes the same value at $\sigma_1$ and at $\sigma_2$. For $2k\ne h$ this is an injective Möbius map of $x^2$, so the linear scattering of the pair preserves the folding exactly when $\sigma_2=\pm\sigma_1$. For $2k=h$ the ratio is $1$ and gives no condition. At $\sigma_2=-\sigma_1$, $\mathbb T^{\rm cl}_k(\sigma)\,\mathbb T^{\rm cl}_{h-k}(-\sigma)=1$, and the pair is transparent. At $\sigma_2=\sigma_1$, with $u=\theta-\theta_d$ and the block (-@eq-fx-block),
$$
